title: Encoding trade-offs and design toolkits in quantum algorithms for discrete optimization: coloring, routing, scheduling, and other problems
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a discrete quantum intermediate representation (DQIR) that is encoding-independent and intended to simplify the specification, analysis, and compilation of discrete (integer-valued) optimization problems for quantum algorithms. It presents a library of primitives and automated tooling for mapping problems to various qubit encodings, provides numerical comparisons of encoding choices across several combinatorial problems, and designs low-depth graph-derived partial mixers (GDPMs) for QAOA, highlighting cases where compact encodings can be competitive or advantageous.
methodology_description: The authors introduce a hardware-agnostic Discrete Quantum Intermediate Representation (DQIR) to express discrete (integer-valued) optimization problems and quantum algorithmic primitives in an encoding-independent way. They define a small set of single-variable primitives (indicator projectors, value/number operators, transfer/shift operators and general local operators) and show how to compose multivariate cost Hamiltonians and non-diagonal mixers from these primitives. The paper proposes algorithmic design patterns (penalties, constraint-preserving mixers, approximate mixers) and a graph-theoretic automatic mixer design called Graph-Derived Partial Mixers (GDPMs). For numerical evaluation, they implemented a Python prototype that: (1) constructs DQIR Hamiltonians for representative problem classes (graph coloring, TSP, machine scheduling, portfolio rebalancing, integer linear programming); (2) maps variables to qubit encodings (standard binary, Gray, unary/one-hot, block-unary) via an integer-to-bit mapping and bitmask subsets; (3) converts DQIR operators to Pauli-string representations; and (4) compiles exponentials of those operators to quantum circuits using a Pauli-Frame-Graph (PFG) product-formula compilation method to obtain circuit depths. They also design strict GDPM mixers via a library-based graph search (Algorithm sketch provided) and decompose multi-qubit gates using known constructions (multi-controlled RY, A_phi, pseudo-Toffoli where applicable). Numerical experiments compute and compare resource metrics (circuit depth and qubit counts, and discuss leakage) for subroutines (primitives, penalties, mixers) and full cost Hamiltonians across encodings and variable domain sizes (d up to 16). All experiments were classical simulations / compilation analyses (no quantum hardware runs).
experimental_setup: Classical simulation/compilation experiments executed on HPC resources (NERSC). Implemented a Python prototype to construct DQIR Hamiltonians, convert them to Pauli strings for different encodings (SB, Gray, unary, block-unary), and compile exponentials using a Pauli-Frame-Graph (PFG) product-formula method to produce quantum circuits and measure circuit depth. Assumed all-to-all qubit connectivity and a gate set consisting of arbitrary single-qubit rotations plus entangling gates (including CNOT). Evaluated variable domain sizes up to d=16 and compared encodings and mixer constructions. No QPU runs.
dataset_used: No real-world financial dataset used. For the portfolio rebalancing example the authors used a toy/synthetic model formulation: 3-state (d=3) discrete asset lots with parameters (covariance matrix σ, mean returns µ, previous portfolio y, budget D, trading cost T, risk parameter λ). Instances are illustrative/synthetic rather than from an external financial dataset.
experiment_input: Synthetic problem instances and small toy parameter sets generated within the prototype. Problem classes tested include: graph coloring (complete graphs with number of nodes equal to number of colors d), traveling salesperson (permutation instances), single-machine scheduling (permutation representations), portfolio rebalancing (d=3 toy model), and canonical integer linear programs. Variable domain sizes d in the experiments ranged from 2 up to 16. No external financial data sources or preprocessing were reported.
experiment_process: 1) Express each problem and required algorithmic primitives in DQIR (encoding-independent). 2) For each choice of qubit encoding (SB, Gray, unary, block-unary), apply an integer-to-bit mapping and derive bitmask subsets for primitives. 3) Convert DQIR operators to Pauli-string sums via automated encoding. 4) For diagonal operators (cost functions, penalties) exponentials are exact since terms commute; for non-diagonal mixers use first-order product-formula approximation (Trotter) or design strict GDPM mixers. 5) Compile Pauli terms to circuits using the Pauli-Frame-Graph (PFG) method to obtain circuit depths; for strict GDPMs, use dedicated decompositions (multi-controlled RY, A_phi, pseudo-Toffoli) to estimate depth. 6) Compare circuit depth and qubit counts across encodings and problems, and analyze leakage behavior for approximate mixers. Parameters explicitly varied: domain size d (2..16), encoding type, choice of mixer (approximate Trotterized shift vs GDPM), and problem class.
experiment_output: Numerical outputs are compilation metrics and analyses: primarily circuit depth and qubit counts for exponentials of primitives, penalties, mixers, and full cost Hamiltonians across encodings and domain sizes. Also qualitative analysis of leakage for approximate mixers and discussion of trade-offs (space vs depth). Results are presented as depth-versus-d plots and comparative summaries; no classical baselines or solution-quality metrics (e.g., objective values or approximation ratios) on quantum hardware were reported.

key_findings: [supported] Introduces DQIR (Discrete Quantum Intermediate Representation), an encoding-independent intermediate representation for discrete (integer-valued) optimization problems that enables compact problem descriptions, algebraic manipulations, and automated mapping to qubit/qudit encodings; a prototype implementation was created.

[supported] Performed numerical comparisons of several encodings (standard binary (SB), Gray, unary/one-hot, and block-unary (BU)) across representative problems (graph coloring, TSP, scheduling, portfolio rebalancing, ILP) and identified encoding-dependent resource trade-offs in circuit depth and qubit count.

[supported] Empirical trend: unary encodings often give the shortest circuit depth for many diagonal primitives and penalties, but compact encodings (SB/Gray) can be substantially better (both in depth and qubit count) in many cases—notably when the variable domain size d is a power of two.

[supported] Block-unary (BU) encodings often interpolate between unary and compact in both space and depth and therefore frequently lie on a space-vs-depth Pareto front for realistic hardware constraints.

[supported] Designed graph-derived partial mixers (GDPMs), including single-variable GDPMs (SB/Gray) up to d≈15, via a graph-theoretic library-search approach; these strict mixers (no leakage) give substantially lower decomposed circuit depths than a naive first-order Trotter implementation of the usual shift-mixer.
[supported] For compact encodings when d is a power of two, the simple binary mixer (product of RX on each encoded qubit) has depth 1 (very low depth) and produces no leakage in that special case.

[supported] Penalty-exchanging (expanding an encoding domain to get a simpler mixer/circuit and adding an encoded validity penalty) can reduce overall circuit depth in certain cases (example: expanding from d=7 -> d=8 and adding a validity penalty reduced depth).

[supported] Provided specific circuit-decomposition and compilation details (used Pauli-frame-graph based compilation/PFG to obtain low-depth product-formula circuits for exponentials), including practical remarks on multi-controlled gate decompositions and when pseudo‑Toffoli variants may reduce depth (with caveats about phases).

[supported] Discussed practical compilation/encoding considerations such as bitmask subsets to exploit locality, mixed encodings (using different encodings per variable), and that encoding choice should be co-designed with hardware resource constraints (depth vs qubit count).

[speculative] The DQIR abstraction, mixed-encoding workflows, and GDPM library are claimed likely to be practically useful to practitioners, aiding automated encoding selection and algorithm design across different hardware (including qudits and fault-tolerant/encoded settings), but broader utility remains to be validated by further studies/experiments.

[speculative] While compact encodings are shown to be "more amenable to QAOA than previously understood" in many of the studied cases, the authors explicitly avoid claiming any statement of quantum advantage or guaranteed performance improvements across all problems/hardware; the general impact on final algorithmic performance is left as future work.
results_summary: This paper presents DQIR, an encoding-agnostic intermediate representation for discrete combinatorial optimization problems, and demonstrates how it facilitates automated mapping to qubit encodings, algebraic simplifications, and resource analyses. Through a prototype implementation and numerical experiments across several example problems (graph coloring, TSP, scheduling, portfolio rebalancing, ILP), the authors compare encoding choices (SB, Gray, unary, block-unary) and show nuanced trade-offs: unary often yields shortest depth for diagonal terms, but compact encodings can be better—especially when domain size d is a power of two—and block-unary often lies between extremes and can be optimal for mid-range hardware. They design graph-derived partial mixers (GDPMs) that are strict (no leakage) and demonstrate these yield lower decomposed circuit depths than naive Trotterized mixers. The work focuses on tooling and resource trade-offs for implementation (depth, qubits), not on demonstrating quantum advantage.
performance_claims: [supported] The simple binary (compact) single-variable mixer (product of RX on each encoded qubit) has circuit depth 1 (and is leakage-free) when the variable domain size d is an exact power of two.

[supported] Multi-controlled-RY gates (used in the unitary library) can be implemented with depth scaling approximately as 2 * N_q (≈ 2 * d for the single-variable constructions referenced), depending on decomposition strategy.

[supported] A standard Toffoli decomposition has been cited with a circuit depth ~12 for a single Toffoli; a 'pseudo‑Toffoli' (phase-congruent) variant can be implemented with depth ~7, at the cost of altered phases.

[supported] The designed GDPM strict single-variable mixers (computed up to d≈15 for SB/Gray) yield substantially lower decomposed circuit depths than the naive first-order product-formula (Trotter) approximation of the exponential of the fully-connected shift mixer (no explicit numeric depths provided here in text, but supported by the paper’s numerical study).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors explicitly refrain from claiming or demonstrating quantum advantage. The paper focuses on representations, compilation toolkits, encoding/mixer design, and resource trade-off numerics (depth and qubit counts). They note that performance and any potential advantage remain open questions and must be tested case-by-case.
limitations: The paper intentionally does not address algorithmic performance or make claims about quantum advantage; it focuses on tooling and representations rather than empirical or provable performance guarantees.
Numerical studies are preliminary and limited in scope (toy instances, all-to-all connectivity assumed); they do not establish general performance or scaling for real-world problems.

Most resource estimates and compilation examples assume all-to-all qubit connectivity and a specific gate model; the framework as presented does not model hardware topology constraints or noise in the numerical results.
The design and compilation of two-variable partial permutation mixers (PPMs) for compact encodings is recognized as challenging and was not exhaustively resolved in this work.
Some constructions (e.g., partial-mixer graphs) have worst-case exponential growth in size; scalability can be an issue when local partial mixers do not suffice.
The domain-wall (DW) encoding was not included in the resource numerics, so its comparative performance is not quantified in this study.

The product-formula (Trotter) based approximate mixers used as baselines can introduce leakage and often yield larger circuit depths than the designed GDPMs; approximation-driven leakage is a practical limitation.
The GDPM search/design procedure may increase compilation time and provides no formal guarantee of success unless the unitary library is sufficiently expressive.
[inferred] The current implementation and experiments assume integer/finite discrete domains mapped per-variable; handling more heterogeneous or structured domains may require additional engineering.
[inferred] The resource and depth comparisons omit noise and error-correction overheads; thus reported depths and trade-offs may be optimistic for realistic noisy devices.
[inferred] Mixed-encoding strategies and mid-algorithm encoding changes are discussed but not fully explored or benchmarked; their practical cost/benefit and toolchain complexity remain unquantified.

[inferred] Many design choices (penalty weights, ordering, parameter setting, etc.) are left to practitioner choice or future tuning — the framework does not provide automated, provably optimal parameter selection.
open_questions: Under which circumstances, for which problems, and to what degree can quantum advantage be achieved for discrete combinatorial optimization?

How does encoding choice (unary, compact SB/Gray, block-unary, domain-wall, mixed encodings) interact with specific hardware constraints (qubit counts, connectivity, native gate set, noise) to determine the best practical implementation?
What are robust, general methods for selecting penalty weights and for trading off penalties versus constraint-preserving mixers (i.e., when to apply penalty exchanging)?
Can efficient, low-depth partial permutation mixers (PPMs) be designed for compact encodings that act on fewer qubits, and do such constructions exist generally?

How do approximate mixers (with controllable leakage) perform empirically in QAOA and related algorithms compared to strict (leakage-free) mixers, considering both circuit depth and overall success probability?
What is the impact of hardware topology and noise (including error-correction overhead) on the resource trade-offs between encodings and mixer choices?
How well do the new GDPM mixers translate into improved algorithmic performance (e.g., in QAOA) on realistic instances and devices?
What are the limitations and practical scalability of the GDPM compilation/search procedures as problem size grows, especially when the mixer graphs become large?
Can the conversion between encodings in the middle of an algorithm (to exploit different strengths at different stages) be done efficiently enough to yield net improvements in resource use?
What are the performance and scaling limitations of quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) and other variational or non-QAOA approaches for discrete combinatorial optimization?
How do pseudo-Toffoli or phase-congruent decompositions affect long-series layered algorithms like QAOA (i.e., what is the effect of phase-errors introduced by cheaper decompositions)?
What are practically effective strategies for automated, instance-aware selection among encodings, mixers, initial states, and penalties within a full-stack compilation workflow?
future_work: Incorporate noise models and hardware topology constraints into the DQIR framework and numerical analyses to obtain more realistic resource and performance predictions.
Extend DQIR and the tooling to support qudit-based hardware, quantum error correction, and fault-tolerant implementations (i.e., map to physical/logical qubits and QEC encodings).
Further investigate and design low-depth two-variable partial permutation mixers (PPMs) for compact encodings, including constructions that operate on fewer qubits.
Explore ancilla-based mixer designs and other advanced mixer primitives (including hybrid penalty-plus-mixer approaches) to handle complex constraints efficiently.

Empirically evaluate the performance of GDPMs and other mixer designs within full algorithms (QAOA, QITE, variational ansätze) on larger and more realistic instances and on hardware or noise simulators.
Study and benchmark penalty exchanging strategies (modifying domains vs adding penalties) in end-to-end algorithm performance, not just subroutine depth.
Develop compilation strategies and gate decompositions optimized for realistic hardware gate sets, including careful treatment of multi-qubit gates and pseudo-Toffoli trade-offs.
Investigate automated selection/tuning of encoding, mixer, initial state, and penalty parameters possibly using classical pre-processing or meta-learning approaches.
Analyze the theoretical and empirical limits of QITE and related imaginary-time or variational methods for combinatorial optimization, including convergence and resource scaling.
Integrate DQIR into wider quantum software toolchains and explore mixed encoding, mid-algorithm encoding conversion, and other compilation optimizations in practice.
key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Introduces DQIR, an encoding-independent intermediate representation to systematically express discrete optimization problems and algorithmic primitives, enabling automated comparison of qubit encodings and circuit compilation costs relevant to NISQ-era resource planning.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Designs Graph-Derived Partial Mixers (GDPMs) as low-depth, constraint-preserving mixers for QAOA-like algorithms and provides strict decompositions to estimate realistic circuit depth.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Provides a numerical compilation study (classical prototype) comparing encodings (standard binary, Gray, unary, block-unary) across problem classes (coloring, TSP, scheduling, portfolio rebalancing) and domain sizes up to d=16, reporting qubit counts and circuit depths.

#limitation:data-encoding — Highlights encoding trade-offs (space vs depth) showing compact encodings can reduce qubit counts but may increase circuit depth or leakage; encoding overheads are central to resource estimates.

#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrates that some encodings (e.g., unary) are qubit-expensive while others (binary/Gray) are qubit-efficient, making qubit availability a primary constraint in mapping discrete problems to quantum circuits.

#limitation:simulation-only — All results are from classical compilation/simulation and circuit-depth estimation (PFG product-formula); no quantum hardware experiments or empirical, hardware-noise-inclusive benchmarks were reported.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — The paper does not present solution-quality metrics (objective improvements or approximation ratios) nor classical performance baselines; resource claims are not validated by hardware runs or end-to-end algorithmic performance.
